title: Rooftop solar: A national asset or a burden on national electricity grid? | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:55
-     - {{hitsCtrl.values.hits}}

Despite benefits, the rapid growth of solar power presents significant operational challenges for electricity utilities, particularly in developing countries where electricity grids are often relatively weak, with limited flexibility and modern control systems

Sri Lanka must recognise the economic and environmental benefits of solar power while addressing the growing technical and financial challenges faced by electricity utilities.

Sri Lanka's electricity sector is undergoing a significant transformation. What began as a modest rooftop solar programme has developed into one of the country's most important sources of renewable electricity. Thousands of households, commercial establishments and industries have invested their own funds to generate electricity, thereby reducing dependence on conventional power plants.

However, this rapid expansion has also created significant challenges for electricity utilities, mainly due to the intermittent nature of solar power generation. When clouds pass over solar installations, electricity generation can drop suddenly and substantially, requiring the utility to immediately compensate for the shortfall to maintain a stable electricity supply. To manage these unpredictable fluctuations, the utility must maintain sufficient spinning reserves, ready to increase generation at short notice, adding to the cost of operating the electricity system. Furthermore, during very sunny weekends, when electricity demand is relatively low, conventional generation has to be reduced to accommodate the high solar output. This can significantly reduce the system's inertia, increasing the risk of frequency instability and making it more challenging to maintain the stability and reliability of the national power system.

The Government's recent decision to discontinue Net Metering and Net Accounting for new rooftop solar connections has therefore raised an important question: Is rooftop solar becoming a financial burden on the electricity sector, or are we overlooking its considerable economic contribution to the country?

The answer requires a comprehensive assessment of both its benefits and its challenges.

Solar power’s growing contribution to Sri Lanka

According to information released by the National System Operator (NSO) in September 2026, Sri Lanka’s total installed solar power capacity exceeded 3,070 MW, comprising approximately 2,542 MW of rooftop solar and 534 MW of ground-mounted solar installations.

Depending on weather conditions, solar generation now contributes approximately 15–25% of the country’s daily electricity requirements. This is a remarkable achievement for a country that remains dependent on imported fossil fuels for a considerable portion of its electricity generation.

In particular, official generation statistics highlight the substantial contribution of rooftop solar to Sri Lanka’s electricity supply. During the first six months of 2026, rooftop solar installations generated approximately 1,228 GWh (1.23 billion units), averaging 205 million units per month or 6.8 million units per day. This represents approximately 13% of the country’s total electricity generation, meaning that nearly one in every eight units of electricity was generated by rooftop solar. To put this into perspective, the energy produced is comparable to the output of a 300 MW power station operating at approximately 94% capacity continuously for six months. This demonstrates the significant role of consumer-funded rooftop solar installations in meeting national electricity demand.

These figures represent a substantial contribution to national electricity supply. Furthermore, rooftop solar electricity consumed directly within households and commercial premises reduces the electricity that must be supplied through the grid, even where this self-consumption is not fully reflected in conventional generation statistics.

It is important to distinguish installed capacity from actual generation. A 1,000 MW solar installation does not generate at full capacity throughout the day, as its output depends on sunlight and weather conditions. With a typical capacity factor (plant factor) of 15–20%, it produces the same amount of electricity over a year as a 150–200 MW power plant operating continuously at full capacity.

Nevertheless, the contribution of solar electricity during daylight hours has become sufficiently significant that the electricity system would face a very different operating and financial situation without it.

Sri Lanka should not approach rooftop solar development as a conflict between electricity utilities and solar investors. Both have an essential role in the country's energy future

The economic benefits of solar generation

One of the greatest benefits of solar electricity is its ability to reduce the amount of electricity generated from conventional thermal power plants.

Every unit of solar electricity that displaces oil- or coal-based generation can reduce fuel consumption. This is especially important for Sri Lanka, where imported fossil fuels create a substantial foreign-exchange burden.

However, the actual economic benefit depends on which generating plant is displaced.

For example, electricity generation costs forecast as per PUCSL Consultation Document for Electricity Tariff Review for 4th Quarter of 2026 approximately:

These figures are reported average costs(forecast) for different sources, not the marginal cost of generating an additional unit at any particular hour. They nevertheless demonstrate why the economic value of solar cannot be determined simply by comparing its purchase tariff with the overall average generation cost.

When solar electricity replaces expensive oil-fired generation, the financial benefit can be considerable. Conversely, when it displaces comparatively inexpensive generation or is produced during periods of excess supply, its immediate economic value may be much lower.

The correct comparison is therefore between the full cost of solar electricity and the actual cost of the electricity that would otherwise have been generated at that time.

This is particularly relevant when evaluating claims that Net Metering creates financial losses for electricity utilities.

Conserving hydropower for the evening peak

Another important benefit is the opportunity to conserve water stored in hydropower reservoirs.

During periods when solar generation is available, it may be possible to reduce hydropower generation and retain water for use during evening peak-demand hours.

This effectively allows hydropower reservoirs to serve as a form of energy storage, although the benefit depends on reservoir levels, water management requirements and whether water would otherwise have been spilled. Such opportunities can reduce the need to operate expensive thermal plants during peak demand.

Solar power also contributes to energy security. During periods of coal plant outages, fuel shortages or reduced hydropower availability, distributed solar generation can reduce daytime demand on conventional generating stations.

Another significant economic benefit of rooftop solar is that the capital investment has largely been borne by households and businesses, reducing the need for government or utility investment in equivalent electricity generation capacity. This contribution of private investment to meeting national electricity demand should also be recognised when assessing the overall economic value of rooftop solar.

The challenges faced by electricity utilities

Despite these benefits, the rapid growth of solar power presents significant operational challenges for electricity utilities, particularly in developing countries where electricity grids are often relatively weak, with limited flexibility and modern control systems. Utilities must continuously balance electricity generation with demand to maintain a stable and reliable power supply. Unlike conventional power plants, solar generation is highly dependent on sunlight and weather conditions, making its output variable and sometimes unpredictable.

One of the major challenges is the changing pattern of electricity demand throughout the day. As rooftop solar generation increases in the morning, demand for electricity from the national grid falls considerably. However, as the sun sets, solar generation declines rapidly while household electricity demand rises, creating what is commonly known as the duck curve. Utilities must therefore maintain sufficient conventional generating capacity to meet the evening peak, even when these power plants operate at reduced output during the day.

Furthermore, sudden changes in solar generation, particularly due to passing clouds, require conventional power plants to increase or decrease their output rapidly. This demands flexible generating capacity, adequate spinning reserves and effective frequency control, all of which involve additional costs. These challenges are particularly serious in smaller and weaker power systems, where limited generation flexibility, low system inertia and inadequate grid infrastructure make it more difficult to maintain stability.

Electricity utilities must remain financially sustainable and maintain a reliable electricity supply. At the same time, renewable energy investors should receive fair compensation for electricity that provides genuine economic value to the national grid. A balanced policy should therefore begin with an independent and transparent assessment of solar power's actual contribution

Voltage rise and reverse power flow

The second major challenge occurs in distribution networks. Traditionally, electricity flows from power stations through transmission and distribution systems towards consumers. Rooftop solar changes this arrangement by allowing consumers to export electricity back into the distribution network. When a large number of solar installations are connected to the same feeder, local generation may exceed local electricity consumption. This can result in reverse power flow, voltage rise, protection coordination difficulties and, in some cases, overloading of distribution transformers or feeders. Excessively high voltage can also cause solar inverters to disconnect automatically, reducing generation and creating further voltage fluctuations.

These are not merely theoretical concerns. The Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL), in its analysis of rooftop solar integration, identified distribution network hosting capacity and inadequate real-time monitoring as major obstacles to further solar expansion.

Following the nationwide blackout in February 2025, additional attention was given to inverter protection settings and grid-support capabilities. The regulator subsequently reported that compliance with updated inverter protection requirements remained inadequate.

It would be incorrect to conclude that rooftop solar alone caused the blackout. However, the incident highlighted the need to develop the grid, modernise power system protection, monitoring and control as renewable energy penetration increases.

The financial challenges: Are net metering and net accounting really causing losses?

Perhaps the most controversial issue is the financial impact of Net Metering and Net Accounting on electricity utilities. Under conventional Net Metering or Net Accounting, electricity exported to the grid can offset electricity imported by the consumer on a unit-for-unit basis. However, electricity exported during the daytime does not necessarily have the same economic value as electricity imported during the evening peak.

A consumer may export solar electricity when relatively inexpensive generation is available, but consume electricity at night when the utility must operate more expensive generating plants. Furthermore, electricity tariffs recover more than the direct cost of energy generation. They also contribute towards transmission and distribution infrastructure, maintenance, system operation and other fixed costs.

As more consumers reduce their net electricity purchases through solar generation, the utility may recover less revenue towards these costs. This can create financial pressure and potentially transfer costs to consumers who do not own solar installations. The concern is legitimate, particularly from the perspective of lower-income households that may not be able to afford rooftop solar.

Nevertheless, a reduction in electricity sales revenue should not automatically be treated as an equivalent financial loss to the utility. The utility must also account for the generation costs avoided because solar electricity is available. If a unit of solar electricity eliminates the need to purchase expensive thermal electricity, there is a real saving that must be included in the calculation. Similarly, where solar reduces system losses, conserves water for hydropower generation or reduces fuel imports, these benefits must be appropriately recognised.

On the other hand, solar generation does not automatically eliminate existing capacity payments, network maintenance costs or the need to retain generating capacity for periods without sunlight. Therefore, the actual financial impact can only be determined by considering all these factors together.

Rethinking net metering and net accounting

In September 2026, the Ministry of Energy directed that new rooftop solar connections and extensions of existing agreements should operate under the Net Plus scheme, rather than the traditional Net Metering and Net Accounting arrangements.

Under Net Plus, electricity generation and electricity consumption are accounted for separately, allowing solar generation to receive an approved payment while electricity purchased from the grid is billed under the applicable consumer tariff.

The Government has justified this change partly on the grounds that electricity exported during the day should not automatically compensate for higher-cost electricity consumed at night. However, the policy has generated considerable concern among solar investors and industry participants.

There is also a regulatory difference of interpretation. In a September 2026 clarification, PUCSL maintained that separate measurement of electricity imports and exports could be implemented without necessarily discontinuing the existing commercial arrangements under Net Metering and Net Accounting.

This disagreement highlights the importance of transparent regulatory decision-making. Policy reforms should recognise the genuine costs associated with solar integration without unnecessarily discouraging private investment in renewable energy.

Before making fundamental changes to Net Metering and Net Accounting arrangements, it would be prudent for the authorities to undertake and publish a comprehensive, transparent cost-benefit assessment of rooftop solar generation. Such an assessment should establish its true economic value to the national electricity system and provide a sound basis for fair and sustainable tariff policies, while protecting existing contractual commitments and investor confidence

Energy storage: An essential part of the solution

Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) and pumped storage hydropower plants can play a vital role in addressing the challenges associated with increasing solar generation. Surplus solar electricity produced during the daytime can be stored and released during evening peak-demand hours, reducing dependence on expensive thermal generation. Batteries can also respond rapidly to sudden changes in generation, helping maintain system frequency, improve grid stability and minimise the curtailment of renewable energy.

The National System Operator (NSO) has outlined plans to introduce approximately 1,240 MW of battery storage capacity, with an energy storage capability of 4,660 MWh, during 2027–2029. However, the location of these storage facilities is equally important. While large batteries connected to grid substations can support overall power system stability, they may not resolve local voltage fluctuations and transformer overloading caused by high rooftop solar penetration. Therefore, a coordinated approach involving grid-scale storage, strategically located distribution-level batteries and consumer-owned storage systems is essential.

In addition, Time-of-Use (TOU) tariffs and appropriate incentives can encourage consumers to use more electricity during periods of abundant solar generation. Activities such as electric vehicle charging, water pumping, industrial processes and other flexible electricity loads can be shifted to daytime hours. This would improve the utilisation of solar electricity, reduce the need for costly storage and conventional generation, and help maintain a more stable and economically efficient power system.

The way forward: A balanced national policy

Sri Lanka should not approach rooftop solar development as a conflict between electricity utilities and solar investors. Both have an essential role in the country’s energy future.

Electricity utilities must remain financially sustainable and maintain a reliable electricity supply. At the same time, renewable energy investors should receive fair compensation for electricity that provides genuine economic value to the national grid.

A balanced policy should therefore begin with an independent and transparent assessment of solar power’s actual contribution. Such an assessment should compare the hourly operating costs of the electricity system with rooftop solar and without rooftop solar, considering avoided fuel expenditure, hydropower reservoir management, network losses, fixed generation costs, capacity payments, energy storage requirements and grid stability.

It should also examine whether existing electricity tariff structures distribute system costs fairly among solar and non-solar consumers.

The longer-term solution requires modernising the distribution network, improving real-time monitoring, enforcing smart-inverter standards and introducing more dynamic tariff arrangements that recognise the changing value of electricity throughout the day.

Rather than relying entirely on uniform restrictions, utilities should assess the capacity of individual feeders and transformers to accommodate additional solar installations. Where technical limitations exist, network reinforcement, improved inverter control and suitable storage solutions should be evaluated.

Finally, any changes to electricity tariffs or connection schemes should be implemented through a transparent, consultative process that maintains investor confidence and protects consumers.

Conclusion

Rooftop solar has become a valuable national energy resource, making a substantial contribution to Sri Lanka’s electricity supply, reducing dependence on imported fuels, conserving hydropower resources under suitable conditions and supporting the country’s transition towards cleaner energy. Equally important, much of this generation capacity has been developed through private investment by households and businesses, reducing the need for government and utility capital expenditure on additional daytime generation.

At the same time, the growing contribution of solar power presents genuine technical and financial challenges for electricity utilities. Its intermittent nature, the need for costly spinning reserves, reduced system inertia during periods of high solar generation, evening peak-demand requirements and limitations in existing distribution networks all require careful attention. The financial sustainability of electricity utilities and the fair recovery of network costs must also be ensured. These challenges, however, should be addressed through appropriate grid development, modern technologies and sound regulatory policies rather than by discouraging further investment in rooftop solar.

The economic contribution of rooftop solar should therefore be assessed from a broader national perspective, considering not only its impact on utility revenue but also the avoided fuel expenditure, reduced foreign exchange requirements, potential savings in public investment, conservation of hydropower resources and environmental benefits. Equally, the additional costs of maintaining grid stability, providing reserve generation, strengthening networks and introducing energy storage must be properly accounted for.

Before making fundamental changes to Net Metering and Net Accounting arrangements, it would be prudent for the authorities to undertake and publish a comprehensive, transparent cost-benefit assessment of rooftop solar generation. Such an assessment should establish its true economic value to the national electricity system and provide a sound basis for fair and sustainable tariff policies, while protecting existing contractual commitments and investor confidence.

Sri Lanka has already made considerable progress in developing rooftop solar through the participation of its citizens and businesses. Preserving this achievement while addressing the legitimate concerns of electricity utilities requires a balanced, long-term approach. The priority should be to strengthen and modernise the electricity grid, introduce appropriate energy storage and encourage better utilisation of solar electricity through suitable tariff incentives.

The challenge before Sri Lanka is not to restrict the growth of solar power, but to develop an electricity system capable of accommodating it safely, reliably and economically. With proper planning and balanced policies, rooftop solar can continue to benefit consumers, electricity utilities and the national economy alike.

(The author is Former Chief Operating Officer, Electricity Distribution Lanka Ltd.,)

title: Sri Lankan University Rankings: The free fall (Part 1) | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:45
-     - 12

On 4 November, Quacquarelli Symonds (QS), the London-based higher education analytics firm, released its Asia University Rankings for 2027. For Sri Lanka, the results made uncomfortable reading. The University of Colombo, still the country’s best-ranked university, dropped 46 places to 364th in Asia. The University of Peradeniya fell to 389th and the University of Sri Jayewardenepura to 398th. Each of the three recorded its lowest placing in four years. Of the 12 Sri Lankan universities ranked, eight went down, two went up and two stayed where they were.

Two years ago, the University of Colombo was 275th in Asia. It has now lost 89 places in two editions. In the global QS World University Rankings, it slipped from the 951–1,000 band in 2025 to the 1,001–1,200 band, where it has stayed for two consecutive years.

I wrote on this subject in these pages in March 2025, under the title “Are Sri Lankan universities not ashamed of their poor global rankings?” That article argued that our universities sit well below where a country with our income and literacy levels should be. Twenty months later, the question is no longer whether we are behind. It is how fast we are falling further behind, and why so few people in positions of responsibility seem to mind.

This article updates the numbers and looks closely at the full QS Asia 2027 dataset – some 1,722 universities from 26 countries and territories – to see what it tells us about Sri Lanka compared with its natural peers: India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam, Thailand and the Philippines.

Why should business care?

University rankings are sometimes dismissed as a vanity exercise for vice-chancellors. That would be a mistake. For a business audience, rankings matter in at least four practical ways.

In short, rankings are a proxy for how the rest of the world values the human capital we produce. That is a business issue, not just an academic one.

A word of caution about rankings

Before going further, a caveat. Rankings are imperfect. Half of the QS Asia score comes from reputation surveys of academics and employers, which favour large, well-known and English-speaking institutions. The weightings are a matter of judgement, and a university that serves its national mission well can still rank modestly. QS has also expanded its tables so quickly that year-to-year rank changes need careful reading.

But these objections cut both ways. Every country in this comparison is measured with the same yardstick, under the same rules, using the same surveys. When countries with similar or lower incomes consistently outperform us on that common yardstick, the problem cannot be explained away as a flaw in the methodology. And whatever academics think of rankings, students, parents, employers and foreign universities use them.

Same income, different league

The most damning way to look at Sri Lanka’s position is against countries with similar or lower incomes. According to the International Monetary Fund’s World Economic Outlook (April 2026), Sri Lanka’s GDP per capita in 2025 was about $ 5,000. That is almost exactly the level of Indonesia ($ 5,082) and Vietnam

($ 4,829). It is nearly double that of India ($ 2,675) and Bangladesh ($ 2,636) and three times that of Pakistan ($ 1,696).

If university standing simply followed national income, Sri Lanka would sit alongside Indonesia and Vietnam, and well ahead of India, Bangladesh and Pakistan. It does neither. Table I, which updates the first table of my 2025 article, sets out the global picture.

The pattern is stark. Every country in the table, rich or poor, has a flagship university ranked in the top 600 in the world. Sri Lanka’s best is outside the top 1,000. Pakistan, with one-third of our per capita income, has 18 universities in the global list, and its best, Quaid-i-Azam University, is at 381st. Bangladesh has 13, led by the University of Dhaka at 600th. India has 52, and IIT Delhi is at 118th. Indonesia, at our income level, has 20 ranked universities with Universitas Indonesia at 191st.

To be fair, not every neighbour is rising. Pakistan’s and Bangladesh’s flagships have slipped in the global table over the last two years, as have those of the Philippines and Vietnam. And Sri Lanka did add one university, Moratuwa, to the global list. But slipping from 315th to 381st, as Quaid-i-Azam did, is a very different problem from being stuck beyond 1,000.

Figure 1 makes the same point using the Asia rankings. Plot each country’s best university against its GDP per capita, and Sri Lanka stands out on its own. Every other country of comparable or lower income, except Nepal, has a university in Asia’s top 160. Ours is at 364.

The great fall: What three years of data show

It would be convenient to blame the decline on QS adding hundreds of new universities to its tables. The Asia list has indeed grown rapidly – from roughly 1,000 institutions in the 2025 edition to 1,529 in 2026 and 1,722 this year. A bigger field means more competitors, and more ways to be overtaken.

However, QS itself has rejected that explanation for Sri Lanka’s latest fall. According to QS data shared with the Daily Mirror, only two newcomers ranked above Colombo or Sri Jayewardenepura this year, accounting for about two places of each university’s decline. The main reason is that regional rivals improved while Sri Lankan scores stood still. A typical university in the table improved its overall score by about 1.7 points; Colombo’s slipped from 39.4 to 39.0 and Sri Jayewardenepura’s from 37.8 to 37.5. In a race, standing still is the same as going backwards.

It is also notable that Sri Lanka had no new entrant at all in 2027. Of the 195 universities that entered the Asia rankings for the first time this year, India contributed 34, Indonesia 22, Vietnam eight, Pakistan seven and Bangladesh six. Sri Lanka contributed none. Our neighbours are widening the base of their systems; we are not.

Table II, which replaces the second table of my previous article, shows how each of the 12 Sri Lankan universities fared this year.

There are bright spots. The University of Moratuwa climbed 37 places to 517th and the University of Kelaniya rose from the 731–740 band to 687th. Moratuwa’s strength in research output per academic – it ranks 335th in Asia on papers per faculty, the best of any Sri Lankan university – suggests what focused, outward-looking institutions can achieve. But the three largest and oldest universities, which carry the national brand, are all moving the wrong way.

The longer view is even more sobering. In the 2019 QS Asia rankings, the University of Peradeniya was 174th and Colombo 188th, albeit in a much smaller field. Both are now well below 350th. In 2022, five Sri Lankan universities were in Asia’s top 200 for employer reputation. Today only Colombo remains, at 192nd.

In the second part of this article, I will look inside the QS data to see exactly where Sri Lankan universities lose their marks, what our peers did differently, and what policymakers, university leaders and the business community can do to reverse the fall.

(The author is a policy researcher cum academic. AI tools including Claude.ai, Perplexity AI and Grok.com have been used in the compilation of the article. The author has validated the facts and takes full responsibility. The ideas expressed are personal. The author can be reached at chanuka@hotmail.com.)

title: One voice, million hearts: Myriad reflections  of a maestro | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:37
-     - 7

Having watched “Rhythm of Guitar,” which was like a Sri Lankan “Mamma Mia,” I expected many to follow in the same genre. From Clarence to Milton, it is amazing how cinema can capture the versatility and vibrancy of valued celebrities. Today’s column is not a conventional movie review but a concentration on “One Voice, One Million Hearts,” from a managerial perspective.

Overview 

“Eda Raa” (“One Voice, One Million Hearts”), is a Sinhala musical movie that appeals to all masses. It is described as a biographical drama film that depicts the true life story of  Milton Mallawarachchi, known as a musical legend with a “magical voice.” Directed by Aruna Jayawardena and produced by Oneline Production and Entertainment in collaboration with Ranil Mallawarachchi, Dr. Arosha Fernando, and Chamaka Manjula, Channa Deshapriya covered the cinematography, with Shan Alvis in charge of editing and color grading. The movie has an amazing screenplay by Suneth Malinga Lokuheva and Priyanath Vidanapathirana, while Suresh Maliyedda provides the brilliant music as usual.

Merry movements of musical movies

“Eda Raa”, like “Rhythm of Guitar” reminds me of many memorable musical movies. Among such classics, “Singin’ in the Rain,” “The Sound of Music,” and “The Wizard of Oz” are often regarded as the most popular. “West Side Story,” “Cabaret,” and “My Fair Lady” also highlight the high impact created by musical movies. Mama Mia is one of the recent ones that created a music sensation. 

Mama Mia is a 2008 musical romantic comedy film directed by Phyllida Lloyd and written by Catherine Johnson, based on her book from the 1999 musical of the same name. The film is based on the songs of pop group ABBA, with additional music composed by ABBA member Benny Andersson. The film features an ensemble cast, including Meryl Streep, Christine Baranski, Amanda Seyfried, Pierce Brosnan, Dominic Cooper, Colin Firth, Stellan Skarsgård, and Julie Walters. The plot follows a young bride-to-be named Sophie (Seyfried) who invites three men (Brosnan, Firth, and Skarsgård) to her upcoming wedding, with the possibility that any of them could be her real father.

Milton moving from “rags to riches” 

Let us move from Mama Mia to Milton. It is indeed amazing to see a village lad who had a painful childhood rising to centerstage as a vibrant vocalist. He was born on 7 April 1944 in Kotte, Colombo. He completed his education at Ananda Sastralaya, Kotte, and got his first job as a bill clerk at the Welikada Co-Operative and later worked as a cashier at the Nawaloka business On 23 December 1973, he married Swarnamala Malathi Panangala, and was blessed with four children, Ranil, Harshini, Nadeeja, and Tharaka. 

At early stages of his singing career, he entertained the audience with popular Hindi songs. He was the vocalist of a musical band called the “Sakyans”, and thereafter the “La Ceylonians” since 1965. He transitioned from not only Hindi songs to Sinhala originals but also from records to cassettes. He is acclaimed as the first Sinhala singer to produce a music cassette. It is interesting to see his mega musical journey from records to cassettes and then to CDs, aptly named as the “Prince of Love Songs.” 

Milton, like many other artists, was much into liquor and cigarettes. Whilst finding solace amidst pressure, he was slowly digging his own grave by sheer neglect of taking care of himself. The movie portrays him as a person who had plenty of fun with his friends, having moved from “rags to riches.” Yet, he had a price to pay. With a brief illness, he  passed away on 10 March 1998 at the age of 53.

Talent in abundance 

Milton’s musical talent was identified as “magic” by many supporters. His voice contained the rare appeal with needed depth and breadth. He was glad to have spotted it by veterans in the Sri Lanka Broadcasting Corporation at that time. He continued to create sensations because of his magical voice, which truly attracted “million hearts.” 

In the movie, Roshan Ravindra portrays the complex character of Milton in a magnificent manner. The magic of Milton’s music was aptly blended with the equal magic of Roshan’s acting. Selecting the right person for the right reason is amply demonstrated here. He is not a stranger to both Cinema and television, with his previous powerful performances. The way he demonstrates the simplicity and seriousness of Milton at the same time from an innocent rural lover to an intense, mature music maestro was simply amazing. 

Apart from Roshan with his ravaging role as Milton, Nethmi Nisheka Roshel Rogers as Swarna, Senali Fonseka as Annette,  and Sheshadrie Priyasad as Shirani have done justice to the assigned roles as the three beautiful women surrounding the life of Milton. Further Biyanka Amarasinghe as Victor Rathnayake, Vishwa Kodikara as Vijeya Kumaratunga and Kalana Gunasekara as Premakeerthi de Alwis rekindle the visual memories we have about the golden times of artistic giants of Sri Lanka.

Way forward 

I remember what Kahlil Gibran said a long time ago. ““Music is the language of the spirit. It opens the secret of life bringing peace, abolishing strife.” The movie “Eda Raa” has done justice to the above statement. It can not only be viewed simply as an entertainment extravaganza but also, we can find several significant aspects beyond the fun. The sweat, tears, frustration, discouragement, longlines and many other negative aspects which can collectively be a poisonous recipe for peril were with Milton as well. How he overcame those in showing his resilience towards revival, was a true embodiment of an endearing person aiming excellence. 

“Music has healing power. It has the ability to take people out of themselves for a few hours,” so said Elton John. Amidst the hustle and bustle of our busy life, “Eda Raa” offers a refreshing relief, resonating with revered memories. For me, it is not only about Milton as a Magical singer but a convincing story about perseverance, persistence, and profound performance.

(The author, a Senior Professor in Management, and an Independent Non-executive Director, can be reached at ajantha@pim.sjp.ac.lk, ajantha.dharmasiri@gmail.com or www.ajanthadharmasiri.info.)

title: David C. Sanders: Master educator, visionary leader, and true friend of Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:29
-     - 9

The news of the passing of David Charles Sanders in the UK on 14 October was received in Sri Lanka with profound sorrow and deep gratitude. A British educator by birth, he served Colombo International School (CIS) for nearly three decades from 1994, leaving an indelible mark on generations of students, staff, and families across both the Colombo and Kandy branches. His exceptional dedication was recognised in 2005 when he was honoured with the national title Sri Lanka Rathna.

Administrative vision and a masterclass in pedagogy 

Succeeding founding principal Elizabeth Moir, Sanders brought sharp administrative vision and a masterclass in pedagogy. Under his guidance, CIS cemented its standing as a premier benchmark for international education. He personally mentored young minds towards Oxford, Cambridge, and leading UK medical schools, and his intellectually rich Monday morning assemblies set a gold standard for school leadership.

Yet it is the human moments that we, his students and colleagues, hold most dear. To us, he was the epitome of a wise, kind, and gentle leader.

Odile Melder, former Head of Drama at CIS, recalled that Sanders never made staff feel managed, but rather supported: “He respected my choices and judgement, giving me a completely free hand during my nine and a half years as Head of Drama. He was more of a father figure, cushioning me from difficulties, always generous with his appreciation, and unfailingly humble.”

Former student Dilruha de Silva remembered his approachable nature and trademark humour: “An extraordinary man who took a genuine, personal interest in the school and the wellbeing of every student. He knew each of us by name and enforced his slightly strict rules with a unique blend of firmness, kindness and fairness. I still laugh remembering him walking around with his foot ruler during intervals and school socials, greeting everyone while ensuring couples maintained a strict 12-inch distance!”

Former Head Girl Niroshi recalled how he listened attentively to her weekly lists of school affairs with quiet amusement: “His athleticism, caring nature, and warm, friendly demeanour were all such defining qualities. His quiet strength and kindness made one feel safe, supported, and looked after. He leaves behind a legacy not only of educational excellence, but of authenticity, quiet wisdom, infectious wit, and genuine, fatherly care.”

Though a British educator, Sanders embraced Sri Lanka as his home in heart and spirit. When my wife Premani organised a Sil program for the CIS Junior School at Sambodhi Vihara, Sanders accompanied us to meet the late Ven. Daranagama Kusaladhamma Thero. Before any of us could remove our shoes, he had already removed his, entering the temple premises with profound respect. He named his home in Dorset “Sri Pada”, and for his daughter’s wedding in the UK, he personally brought a traditional Kukula Pahana, so that a symbol of Sri Lanka might shine at the ceremony.

David C. Sanders

Legendary vitality 

His vitality was legendary. On annual expeditions to World’s End and Sri Pada, he led from the front with energy to spare. On one descent from Sri Pada, he and the front group took a wrong turn towards Ratnapura — a seven-hour walking detour that became a cherished school legend. He was also a familiar figure across Colombo, leaving everyone in his dust as he jogged through the streets in the evenings.

Beyond his academic standing, David possessed a rare personal warmth. He nurtured students not merely for examination papers, but for the world of work, entrepreneurship, and principled citizenship. The lives of my own children — and thousands of alumni globally — stand as enduring proof of his mentorship. At the conclusion of his funeral service in Dorset, he chose to play the CIS anthem as he departed: a final, poignant farewell to the school community he cherished.

As we gather at The Cathedral of Christ the Living Saviour today (9), at 6:00 p.m. for a Service of Thanksgiving and Remembrance, we celebrate the life of an extraordinary leader, an exceptional mentor, and a true gentleman.

May he rest in eternal peace.

(The author is former President, The National Chamber of Commerce of Sri Lanka and Founding Vice Chancellor, Uva Wellassa University)

title: Series of no-hopers begins at Rawalpindi today | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:21
-     - 5

Sri Lanka Captain Kusal Mendis (left) and Pakistan Captain Babar Azam with the trophy that will be awarded to the winner of the two-Test series

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

Sri Lanka placed 7th and Pakistan placed 9th and last, begin a two-Test series at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium today with neither side having any chance of making it to the final of the World Test Championship at The Oval on June 2027. 

Sri Lanka’s campaign has been disappointing so far, with just one win in six Tests. Three draws have offered some protection, but the second half of the campaign demands a dramatic turnaround. For Sri Lanka to make it to the top two they require almost a perfect run – six potential victories in their remaining six Tests.

Sri Lanka’s cricket has been so vulnerable that such a challenge does not look feasible. Even playing matches at home they are unable to convert home advantage into victories as their last series in the WTC indicate. They lost the two-Test series to India 1-0 (1 drawn) and before that they managed only a 1-0 win (1 drawn) against Bangladesh. So, of the three series they have played so far, Sri Lanka has managed to win only one – against Bangladesh and lost two to West Indies (1-0, 1 draw) and to India.

With only 33.33% points from their first three series, Sri Lanka have far too much to do in the second half of their WTC campaign. Even if they win each of their remaining six Tests (2 v Pakistan - away, 2 v New Zealand - away, 2 v South Africa - home) they’ll end up on 66.67%. If they lose one, they’ll drop to 58.33, which is insufficient for them to finish in the top two of the WTC standings.

Their remaining three series of the WTC comprises two away (in Pakistan and in New Zealand) and one at home (against South Africa). Sri Lanka’s record overseas is not a healthy one and their last win in Pakistan came as far back as 2004 when under the captaincy of Marvan Atapattu they won by 201 runs at Faisalabad. The last time Sri Lanka toured Pakistan in 2019 they lost the two-Test series 1-0 (1 drawn). Sri Lanka’s last tour to New Zealand in 2023 saw them being swamped 2-0.

Thus, the odds are stacked heavily against Sri Lanka winning all their last six matches of the WTC.

Pakistan on the other hand have played almost twice as many Tests as the points they have gathered 4.63% and with only four Tests remaining (2 v Sri Lanka – home, 2 v New Zealand – home) says enough about their dire campaign. They are virtually out of the running.

Even in the ICC Men’s Test Rankings there is little that these two teams can achieve. Sri Lanka are placed 7th with 75 rating points and Pakistan 9th with 71 rating points. If Sri Lanka wins the series they will move one slot up to 6th displacing Bangladesh, a win for Pakistan will see them move up to either 6th or 7th position.

In the context, this series will be ideal to groom some of the youngsters in preparation for the next WTC cycle. Sri Lanka has a few of them knocking on the door like middle order batsman Pavan Rathnayake, and wicket-keeper batsman Anjala Bandara – both products of Mahanama College and playing for CCC in the domestic competitions. 

Already Sri Lanka’s future generation of cricketers are beginning to take shape in the Test team with Pasindu Sooriyabandara, Sonal Dinusha and Keshara Nuwantha breaking into Test cricket this year. Bandara has been picked for the two-Test tour to Pakistan as a reserve wicket-keeper to Kusal Mendis. Whether the extra responsibilities of having to captain his country and being wicket-keeper for all three formats is proving to be a burden on Mendis is a matter of conjecture. Mendis, who will be leading his country in a Test match for the first time, certainly could not get going in the recently concluded One-Day Tri-Series in Pakistan where his contribution was only one fifty in five innings. He was thrice dismissed for single digit scores.

For the upcoming Test series against Pakistan, Mendis could simply hand over his wicket-keeping gloves to Bandara and concentrate on leading his team and scoring runs which he is quite capable of. He will be less free from pressure. But that is unlikely to happen as it would unsettle the batting line-up with one of the key batters having to make room for Bandara.

With Pasindu Sooriyabandara promoted from no. 3 to open the batting with Lahiru Udara, the rest of the batting will comprise Dinesh Chandimal, Kamindu Mendis, Dhananjaya de Silva, Sonal Dinusha and Kusal Mendis.

The three-day warm-up game where the PCB Patrons XI fast bowlers creamed off the top order in both innings indicates the type of pitches Sri Lanka will encounter for the two Tests at Rawalpindi and Lahore. 

But Kusal Mendis at the pre-match press conference said his batsmen were capable of handling any type of pitches Pakistan prepares for the Test series.

“We have a very good batting line up with senior players like Dinesh Chandimal, Dhananjaya de Silva and myself along with a couple of others. Everyone knows how to play on green tops. We played very well in England also. I have no doubt in my batting line up,” said Mendis.

Sri Lanka are most likely to opt for three fast bowlers and one spinner. Asitha Fernando and left-armer Dilshan Madushanka are likely to play leaving the option of third seamer to uncapped Eshan Malinga, Lahiru Kumara or fast bowling all-rounder Milan Rathnayaka. For spin, it will be a toss-up between the experienced Prabath Jayasuriya and fast improving off-spinner Keshara Nuwantha.

title: Crucial goalkeeping error costs Sri Lanka match, draws against Bhutan | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:16
-     - 3

Wasim Razik (left) celebrating after scoring the second goal for Sri Lanka

By Althaf Nawaz reporting from Dhaka, Bangladesh

A basic goalkeeping error by Sujan Perera deprived Sri Lanka of certain victory against Bhutan at the 15th SAFF Football Tournament played at the National Stadium in Dhaka, Bangladesh under lights yesterday, and the match ended in a 2-all draw after Sri Lanka had led 2-1 at halftime.

With his vast experience as a goalkeeper, Sujan saved a penalty kick in the second half, but failed to clear two kicks at goal at a crucial stage of the game as he opted to tap the ball into play instead of collecting the ball, and the opponents gleefully pounced on the ball to score. A win here would have secured Sri Lanka a berth in the semi-final on the 14th since Bhutan had already lost to Bangladesh 1-0 a few days back.

Sri Lanka dominated proceedings until the 33rd minute, when Bhutan broke the deadlock following a defensive lapse that gifted them the opening goal. However, the Lankan Lions responded in spirited fashion, with Oliver Källard stealing the limelight by unleashing a spectacular equaliser that left the Bhutanese goalkeeper with no chance of making a save.

Just before the half-time whistle, Sri Lanka surged ahead through a perfectly timed header by striker Wasim Razik, who brilliantly converted a cross delivered by Oliver Källard. The Bhutanese goalkeeper was once again left helpless as the ball found the back of the net, giving Sri Lanka a deserved 2-1 lead at the break.

Bhutan equalised midway through the second half and, buoyed by the equaliser, put added pressure on the Lions. However, Lankan players rose to the occasion and their defence was rock solid, but Lady Luck deserted them and they failed to score even in five minutes of extra time.

In the earlier game, Pakistan defeated Maldives 3-0.

title: ‘Clicky Ponting’ handed two-year suspension over cricket cheating scandal | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:09
-     - 0

The player has now been suspended from playing, coaching, umpiring, scoring and managing junior teams at all levels until September 29, 2028

The English amateur cricketer who went viral for finger-clicking trickery has been handed a two-year suspension, the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League has said.

The fielder Brian Devine, dubbed “Clicky Ponting” on social media in a nod to former Australia captain Ricky Ponting, was accused of tricking umpires by clicking his fingers to make the sound of a ball nicking the bat as deliveries were missed and caught by the wicketkeeper.

The video footage went viral on social media and made international headlines earlier this year. A three-person disciplinary panel reviewed the ‌footage and considered player interviews and written statements before imposing the ban.

“The player concerned is suspended from all cricket under the ECB’s (the England and Wales Cricket Board) jurisdiction for two years, from 30 September 2026 to 29 September 2028. This covers playing, coaching, umpiring, scoring and managing junior teams,” the NYSDL said in a statement on Friday.

Additionally, Saltburn Cricket Club have been fined 300 pounds ($ 402.87) and their second XI has been relegated to Division Three of the NYSDCL and will start the 2027 season with a 60-point deduction, the league added.

Devine and Saltburn admitted the charges, but the club appealed against their sanction. Saltburn said in a statement reported on gazettelive.co.uk: “The club fully participated in the disciplinary proceedings and accept the decision of the appeal following the original decision from the league.”

title: Softlogic Life tees off ‘7 Club Swing’ at Royal Colombo Golf Club | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 03:06
-     - 4

Softlogic Life, hosted the inaugural “7 Club Swing” golf stableford tournament on 17 October 2026 at the Royal Colombo Golf Club. 

The event marked two firsts: the first time an insurer in Sri Lanka has taken on golf, and the first time the seven-club format has been introduced to the country. A select group of valued customers and corporate partners came together for a day of competition, camaraderie and a shared passion for the game.

The tournament opens a new chapter in Softlogic Life’s approach to customer engagement and extends its long-standing ‘Honda Leda’ philosophy. Through ‘Honda Leda’, or “good sicknesses”, the brand has consistently encouraged Sri Lankans to pursue passions that support physical and emotional wellbeing, and more recently has reinforced that age should never stand in the way of one’s ‘Honda Leda’.

Golf was a natural expression of that thinking. It is played and enjoyed across generations and combines fitness, strategy, focus, competition and social connections. With the 7 Club Swing, Softlogic Life set out to inspire people to pursue a passion they can enjoy at every stage of life, and to build strong connections on and off the course. The seven-club structure asks players to complete their round with half the standard set of clubs allowed in the bag. It rewards creativity, shot-making and adaptability over equipment, which makes the game engaging for players of every age and skill level. The tournament was held at the Royal Colombo Golf Club, an institution whose history stretches back to the beginnings of organised golf in Sri Lanka.

Managing Director Iftikar Ahamed said: “Insurance is ultimately about enabling people to live the best quality of life and pursue the life they aspire to. That belief extends beyond providing protection. It also means understanding what our customers value and creating meaningful opportunities to connect with them around those interests. The 7 Club Swing brings that philosophy to life by celebrating a passion that transcends generations, while giving us an opportunity to strengthen relationships with customers and partners in a setting that is engaging, personal and memorable.”

The experience extended beyond the course, with online games and digital engagement activities building excitement and encouraging participation around the tournament. Following the day’s competition, golfers and guests came together for an afternoon of great vibes, music and networking, creating further opportunities to connect in a relaxed setting. Staying true to its promises, Softlogic Life ensured at the vibrant awards ceremony that almost every customer who took part walked away with something in hand. More than 40 gifts and surprises were presented throughout the day, including seven air tickets to Melbourne, Hanoi, Dubai, Delhi, Kuala Lumpur, Hong Kong and Singapore, a Samsung S26, hotel stays and dining experiences. A Hole-in-One Challenge raised the stakes further, with a Ranger vehicle sponsored by Allianz offered as the grand prize.

EVP/Chief Distribution Officer – Alternate Channel Piyumal Wickramasinghe said: “Golf gives us a great setting to spend time with our customers and partners outside the usual business environment. As Sri Lanka’s leader in global, local and corporate health insurance, we partner with many of the country’s leading organisations to protect their people. Being with Softlogic Life means more than access to world-class healthcare. It means access to a global lifestyle. The 7 Club Swing is an expression of that promise: bringing people together around a shared passion, enjoying the day and strengthening the relationships we have built over time. For us, that personal connection is just as important as the solutions we provide.”

For Softlogic Life, The 7 Club Swing reflects an approach to customer relationships that goes beyond conventional insurance interactions. By creating experiences around the passions its customers actively pursue, the Company aims to build connections that are more personal, relevant and enduring, and to show that staying active and doing what one loves remain central to living well at every stage of life.

title: Khawaja claims entire Australia team knew about 2018 ball-tampering scandal | Daily FT
summary:
Monday, 9 November 2026 02:59
-     - 5

Former opener Usman Khawaja claimed on Saturday that the entire Australian team knew about the 2018 “Sandpapergate” scandal in Cape Town and said they also employed the tactic during the previous Test at Port Elizabeth.

Captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Cameron Bancroft were sent home in disgrace and found by a Cricket Australia investigation to be the only three players with prior knowledge of the ball-tampering plot.

Smith was banned for a year and sacked as skipper, Warner was suspended for 12 months and stripped of all leadership roles, while Bancroft was slapped with a nine-month ban. Head coach Darren Lehmann was cleared of direct involvement but resigned soon after the series.

But Khawaja, who retired this year after 88 Tests, told The Sydney Morning Herald everyone had prior knowledge.

“It was all of us. Not the batters, not the bowlers, not the staff. All of us,” he said ahead of the release of his autobiography this  week, where a chapter is dedicated to the issue.

Bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon all denied publicly in 2021 that they knew about it.

Khawaja said he spoke in the dressing room after the Cape Town Test, urging the team to take collective responsibility, rather than scapegoating Warner, Smith and Bancroft.

“In an ideal world, I don’t want to do this,” Khawaja said. “I don’t want to be the one who comes out and talks about the truth. The issue is that I genuinely thought after eight years the truth would have been out by now. Maybe I thought Davey [Warner] would have exposed it, or someone else would have talked about it more. I just didn’t think it was going to come down to this.” In the book, according to the newspaper, Khawaja recounts that discussions about ways to rough up the ball were also held in the dressing room during the second Test at Port Elizabeth, now known as Gqeberha.

It culminated in the discovery that sandpaper was effective, and at this point Smith allegedly walked away, saying he did not want to know about it.

Bancroft then allegedly volunteered to use sandpaper in South Africa’s first innings in Gqeberha, where the ball swung significantly.

Cricket Australia said in a statement it was “comfortable” with the findings of its original investigation, but remained open to new evidence.
